Blood in the Water

At the bottom of Lake Amaya, I discovered the wreck of a small ship and a business ledger that told the tale of a feud between two sea-faring "merchants." According to the footnotes, a series of bottles, containing poetry, and a pair of lucky dice were lost beneath the waves. Perhaps, using the ledger as my guide, I can retrieve the lost items by retracing their voyage from Dagon Fel, across the Sheogorad coastline, and down the Bitter Coast.

In Dagon Fel, I learned that a group of smugglers, disguised as merchants, failed to unload their cargo with the locals. Their presence was tolerated briefly before being run out of town. As they sailed away, they threw empty bottles at the residents. Perhaps in a fit of rage at being cast out, one of those bottles might’ve contained one of the bard's poems...

Among the numerous bottles resting at the bottom of the sea, I found one stuffed with a hand-written note. It contained no poetry, as the priest had claimed, but rather told the tale of a young man whisked away from a life of debauchery by his uncle. No mention was made of their next course, but I do recall the priest making some mention of it in his ledger. I should review his footnotes.
I found another message from the bard, but it was severely damaged due to water seeping into the bottle. Only the words “Omen,” “we,” and “dur” remained legible in the text. Was this a poem?
Beneath the shadow of the ship known as the Omenwedur, I found another bottled message full of sea shanties, mentioning the time Vivec defeated the Ruddy Man. Was this their next destination?

The bard spoke of taking a walk through Koal Cave to "get ideas" on how to further taunt the priest into doing something stupid, while not rousing the orc’s own fury by betraying the group’s bond of trust. What was he doing there swimming after dark?

At the bottom of a pool, I found another bottled message and a pair of dice that glint with magical properties, thus uncovering the last fragment of the story that led to the eventual murder of the bard and the sinking of their ship at Lake Amaya.
The Old Man of the Sea

At the far reaches of the Bitter Coast, I met a nameless castaway, lounging about the rotted planks of a shipwreck. While we traded stories, he made mention about the neighboring shipwrecks, pointing out how strange it was that so many would be destroyed in close proximity of each other, as though something lurked far below the waves.

The nameless castway told me that smugglers had tried and failed to smuggle several of Tashtego’s artifact into Vvardenfell. A dread curse wrought into each of the items might've been the source of their ill-fated doom.

I recovered all of Tashtego’s spear and finally learned the truth concerning its owner. And despite the sad origins, I’ve been tasked with forging ahead with them, creating new adventures to spin and weave into the many myths and legends that wave across the Inner Sea.

While exploring the cabin of a grounded ship, a bone-crunching snap, followed by screams and the heavy thud of ebony maces echoed all around me, causing the wooden planks to creak and groan. Was this brought on by this golden spear? Or was it a mere coincidence?

I told the old castaway how I survived an ambush by a swarm of land dreugh, and in return he gave me his helmet, claiming that such an item would be wasted on him. At long last, he’s revealed his face, leaving me with more questions, rather than answers to his true identity.
I was in no mood to retell my tale against the dreugh swarm.
While exploring a sunken ship, something swam past the hull like a cloud shadow, then disappeared without so much as a sound...

I spent sometime recounting my encounter with the ancient cephalopod that attacked the Hlaalu cargo ship, and in return, the nameless castaway rewarded me with a dreugh spear. The old man told me that if I had anymore nautical adventures to share with him, he’d be willing to trade again.
I refused to share my story with the old man.

Yes, I heard he was quite the knave of hearts! His words might’ve charmed the southern cities, but out here in the frontier, men and women aren’t easily seduced by such fancy wordplay. Here in Dagon Fel, we seek men and women who can hunt, kill, and skin an animal, rather than repeat poetic verses. We chased him and the rest of his crew mates out of town. As they sailed away, they threw empty bottles at us! That much I know is true, since I saw it with my own eyes!

It’s been awhile, yes... few weeks, perhaps. Hard to tell when the days roll together so peacefully like the waves lapping against these foreign shores. I do recall seeing a ship pass by some time ago... yes, a sturdy, sea-worthy ship. I was out in the shallows, trousers rolled up to my knees, harpooning fish when I saw it. I waved at them and a greasy-haired Dunmer returned the gesture, then threw a bottle my way. I swam after it and retrieved it. It wasn’t much, save a few drakes and some bitter wine.
[He laughed heartily.] I have two feet, don't I?

Ah, that’s a sad tale, eh? He went from deckhand to legend before he was fully a man, and was robbed of a peaceful retirement before he’d seen his first gray hair! But... that’s the way of things, no? One can reach great heights, pierce the very skies with your spear, only to have the gods casts you back into the watery abyss without a potion or a spell to soften the blow.

Are you sure you're not retelling an ol’ yarn? Tashtego speared the eye of an ancient cephalopod, so the sailors say. He was a mere boy back then, but I suppose we can’t all be born legends, eh? But what am I saying! This is your story! And even if it sounds vaguely familiar, I had quite the time listening to it. Here, as promised, have this spear I dug out of a corpse’s chest in return for that harrowing tale.
If that's your wish...
[You tell your story to the old, nameless castaway, who sits idly on the wooden planks, drinking his bitter wine and saying little, save to grunt a sign of acknowledgment.]

[He glances at your attire, laughing heartily.] So, I see you’ve gotten yourself inked by a cephalopod, eh? Don’t worry, the stench isn’t permanent and will dissipate in a week or two... maybe a month, if you’re lucky enough. And here you thought those Telvanni helmets were nothing more than gaudy trappings, huh? The sea’s full of mysteries beyond our scope, lass. But enough of that! Come! Have a seat here beside me and tell you about it, no? I’m willing to trade for a good story!

[He glances at your attire, laughing heartily.] So, I see you’ve gotten yourself inked by a cephalopod, eh? Don’t worry, the stench isn’t permanent and will dissipate in a week or two... maybe a month, if you’re lucky enough. And here you thought those Telvanni helmets were nothing more than gaudy trappings, huh? The sea’s full of mysteries beyond our scope, son. But enough of that! Come! Have a seat here beside me and tell you about it, no? I’m willing to trade for a good story!

While we rotted away, entombed beneath the waves, Tashtego’s stories kept our sanity as we slowly were withered away by death, starvation, and other unmentionable fates. I suppose in my ol’ age it’s the least I can do for him - survivor’s guilt, eh? Who knows? Best not dwell on it... Nothing I can do about now, huh? My time draws to an end, friend, and I know charge you with these artifacts to spin new adventures across the Inner Sea. Here, before you go, let me show you a trick or two...

So, you’ve found all of Tashtego’s artifacts, eh? It’s good they’re in your hands, rather than smugglers - curse or no curse. Keep ‘em. They’re off no use to this ol’ deck hand... but I suppose after all that effort you should get some shred of truth out of me, eh? Well, for starters: no, I’m not him. That much is true, but I knew him well. He was my cellmate in the dreugh's court, but he died before we could escape.

Once the king’s court was clouded in blood, Tashtego masked his escape and swam toward the surface with his bride-to-be. However, even as the sun’s light came clear through the waters, a dying dreugh clamped down on his left foot and sheered it off by the ankle. This is how Tashtego the Red became Tashtego the Maimed. It’s a name now uttered in reverence by sailors all across the Inner Sea to ward off vicious storms and other scaled monstrocities. "By Tashtego!" they’d call out from the stem to stern.
Bah! You’ve no appreciation for the craft of storytelling, eh? I’ve not even begun. Would you rather I skip to the last act, before setting the scene? I think you'd better leave.

He’s been dead for near a century, but his legend still thrills and excites those brave enough to challenge the Inner Sea. Tashtego was a mere deckhand who gouged the eye of an ancient cephalopod with a broken mast! As a man he wrestled a she-fish for three days and three nights, before she conceded to be his bride. And when she was stolen by a jealous dreugh king soon afterwards, Tashtego dove into the blackened abyss, armed with nothing more than a golden spear and butchered the entire court.

I’m sure. I’m old, as you can see from this battered face of mine. I’m scarred and weather-beaten. So what good is a sturdy helm to someone like me? Here alone and far from civilization? I’ve lived my life and now I seek peace and tranquility, not blood and destruction; though those stories still excite me as a young man’s dreams. Now, go on! Go! Get off my island! I’m eager to hear more of your future adventures!

Now that’s a song worthy of a shanty, if I say so myself! All that it was missing was a lass or two! And that’ll come! Yes! It’ll come with each mouth that repeats the story and revises it. So don’t be surprised, my friend, if in the near future those sour-faced Ordinators are replaced with scantily-clad wenches! Keep this up, you’ll rival Tashtego himself in infamy! But before that can happen, you’ll need to protect that head of yours... here, take this helmet...

In life, a man may gain much and lose little, but in the end it’s the stories he shared and the stories he helped create that’ll live on beyond their own physical forms. You’d best be on your way... I’m out of wine and in no mood to talk.

[You rise to your feet, telling the story how you fought side by side alongside Ordinators against a swarm of land dreughs. You imitate the sound of bones crunching between claws, while mimicking the chops, slashes, and gut-wrenching thrusts that turned the tide against this sudden assault from the deep.]

[He glances at your equipment.] That spear looks familiar... how’d you manage to find one of Tashtego the Red’s artifacts? The one that turned him into the Maimed at that! There’s a strange tale attached to its acquisition, yes? Please, have a seat and entertain this old man for a little while.

I’ve heard smugglers have managed to steal and distribute several artifacts that once belonged to the famed Dunmer harpooner, Tashtego the Red. However, it seems the curse that was laid upon these artifacts has struck again and many ships have been lost beneath the waves in the attempt to pawn them in Vvardenfell.

Not far from here, there’s two shipwrecks... one’s run aground, another capsized down below. Rather odd, ain’t it? I hear there’s a third not too far from here, though I can’t see it. But that’s rather strange, eh? So many ships, so little distance... maybe these waters are cursed. Or maybe these something in these waters, tearing them apart. For me and my part, I'll stay put, here among the shallow end of the Inner Sea.
How much of this is true, it’s hard to tell, since much of the story’s already been washed through the rumor mill several times by now.

A group of smugglers, trying to pass off as merchants, tried to sell their goods not long ago. Ha! Most people think we Nords are too stupid to see through such a ruse, but it was obvious that they weren’t who they say they were... Hmm, if I remember correctly, one of them had a long, sour expression, like that of a priest... the other was a thin, greasy-haired bard who tried to seduce every man and woman in town!

All around me, blood splattered the walls and bones crunched under my heavy fists! Before long, I must’ve slain three or four men in my wake, including one of the city’s guard. I dashed toward the door, down the flight of steps, and leapt into the darkness of the nearby river. I swam until my arms and legs ached and was set adrift by the sea. When I awoke, my eye was infected and beyond saving. So! I plucked it out! And I tell you, friend, there’s no pain that truly compares to tearing out your own eye!

Ah, so you want to know about the eye, eh? Well, there’s not much to tell. Unlike those heroes in sailor’s tales, who always lose a limb in some storm-drenched battle, I lost this eye when a wench at the House of Earthly Delights threw a dart at my face, mistaking it for the scoreboard. In my anger, I struck her, only to realize she wasn’t drunk, but knee-deep in skooma. Her friend, however, didn’t accept my apologies and a fight ensued.
How'd I lose it? That's a story for another time, when I'm in a better mood to daydream about she-demons!
You simply can’t get good work these days... you’d think these slaves would be perfectly suited for such a task, but they spend more time splashing about like children...

What now? Don’t you see I’m busy watching over these lazy slaves? Hey! You! Dimwit! Stop paddling about in the water and dive down there and fill that basket! Now! This isn’t a Black Marsh tide pool! Get to work!
You’ve returned? And you’re still alive and well. Clearly, you haven’t been lured by the prospect of making a fortune here; otherwise you’d be a lump of blackened ash by now.

In accordance to maritime laws, House Telvanni has laid claim to this wreckage. You are free to observe, but know that we will not hesitate to incinerate you with a spell, if you decide to turn from a casual observer to an underhanded brigand. Most of the ship’s crew has already met this fate and now rest beneath the waves, black and charred, as it ought to be for such bottom-feeding scoundrels.
Leave. Now. I’ll not ask again, %PCRace.
You’re asking for trouble, aren’t you?
I warned you, %PCName! Don't test my patience...
That's quite enough, %PCRace! I’ll not have my authority undermined by such ignorance of the law!

I don’t know you, nor do I care to know you! This shipwreck is a private matter and does not concern you! Leave. Now. Unless you wish to have your head caved in like these smugglers! It’s your choice, %PCRace.
Greetings, lass! Aren’t you a sight for sore eyes!

I’d greet you properly, but I prayed for a beautiful lass to swim out of the sea; instead, I have you, and you look rougher than a sturgeon’s scales! And instead of that, I was blessed with your ugly face and briny stench!
Where are the mer-maids and mer-men, huh? I once read about nymphs and harpies in Daggerfall, but where are the nymphs and sirens of the Inner Sea?

If you’re aiming to sail the Inner Sea, you need to learn to respect it, fear it, and above all else, never speak ill of it. The Sea has no ears, but she listens... yes, she listens. With each swell of the waves, with each foamy crash against the sand and the jagged rocks, she listens... The Sea is not a harsh mistress. No. The Sea is a harsh, loving wife with an 'ear' to the floorboards, waiting for the smallest slight against her good nature.

Sometimes I sit here and wonder... is there anything better and more symbolic of life's struggles than a man and his fishing rod? The drawing, the pulling, the endless battle for life, the endless angler stories... oh? You're here. Again. What do want now? Can't an old man muse in peace these days, huh? Can't think of fishing and bait without interruption... where was I? Should I use glowbugs this time? Meat? An old shoe, perhaps?

Curious about these bits of armor? I found them... yes, found them! On a corpse, you see, floating south along the Bitter Coast. It was a lucky find to say the least, since I only had these rags to protect me. And before you ask who he was, it’s impossible to tell. After all, who can identify a man who’s head had been cleared off its shoulders by slaughterfish!

I’ve a few goods I’ve fished out the sea bottom, if you’re interested. I can guarantee a fair trade, but I can’t guarantee they’re free of that briny stench that often accompanies watery treasures. But a good trade is a good trade, no?

You’re the strangest thing I’ve seen crawl out of the ocean today! You’re not a fish, nor a bird, or a corpse. So, what could you be, eh? A scaly riddle indeed. I hope the answer isn’t a thief or a cutthroat! I’d hate to have to wash the blood off these planks again...

Oh, it’s you again... don’t you see I’m busy pondering the secrets of turning roots, mushrooms, and fish scales into wine? Can’t an old man just sit here, watching the sun rise and fall, without being rudely interrupted every five minutes?

Come to trade tales with an ol' man, eh? Come! Have a seat! Throw back a few swigs of this bitter wine with me! Let’s sit back and watch the clouds, the sun, and the moons move about in the sky, while we tell tales and sing bawdy songs. It’s been quite some time since I’ve spoken with another and today’s a good day for it, I think.

Me? I’m merely another sailor on the seas of fate, cast away and set adrift as driftwood from another time; half-forgotten by many who still make sail across the Inner Sea, and half-remembered by fewer still. And as for my name... well, I’m afraid to say that my own name escapes me at the moment, but what do names, titles, and prestige matter for an ol’ man like me? I seek nothing and want nothing, save peace and tranquility.
Why would I trust something that just swam out of the sea? For all I know, you could be a dreugh or even worse a slaughterfish in disguise!

Name’s Ylgor Cold-Hands. I’m a deckhand mostly, but I’ve been known to work other jobs as well. Out here in the frontier, so far from the larger trade routes, we Nords can’t really afford to remain still in one occupation. We have to adapt to the circumstances to ensure our survival. I’ve been a deckhand, a blacksmith’s apprentice, a laborer, a farmer, a cook, a tanner, and even a midwife!

Ha! When I was younger, the local mid-wife had grown ill, so my father "volunteered" me into becoming one. I knew how to raise animals, so I was somewhat familiar with the process. And so, even before I was man, I'd already delivered a handful of children. However, each woman I'd helped give birth, complained furiously that my hands were as cold as a draugr!
